newsitem.title: GERMANY: BMW seen racing toward higher H1 profits.
newsitem.headline: BMW seen racing toward higher H1 profits.

text.p: German luxury carmaker Bayerische Motoren-Werke AG (BMW) will show profits on a steady upward course when the company reports first-half results later this week, car industry analysts said on Monday.

BMW, which saw profits climb 18.5 percent in 1996, is riding a wave of popular models, but also got a helping hand in the first half from factors beyond the control of company strategists in Munich, analysts said.

Analysts said on average that the strong U.S. dollar would help lift BMW's first-half net profit to around 400 million marks ($217 million) and sales to 29 billion marks -- compared to profits of 335 million marks and sales of 25.2 billion marks in the first half of 1996.
"Clearly sales are going quite well," said Christoper Will, analyst at Lehman Brothers in London. "Earnings will climb solidly."
The carmaker has not set a specific date for the release of the figures, but said it will announce results for the first six months sometime this week.

Although there is no denying that BMW has captured the market's attention with popular, technologically advanced models, analysts said the real story during the first half of 1997 was the mark's dive against the dollar and a low comparison figure in the first of last year.
The dollar has climbed 19.60 percent against the mark so far this year to 1.8458, boosting sales and profits by increasing the mark value of business conducted in the huge U.S. market.
Although the strong pound could be bad news for BMW's British-based Rover Group unit, analysts said on balance the currency impact clearly is in the group's favour.

Analysts such as Salomon Brothers' John Lawson, meanwhile, said the results could get a further lift because sales were sluggish in the first half of 1996, making the first half of 1997 look strong in comparison.
The first half of 1996 was unusually difficult for BMW as it updated its 5-Series model, replacing its executive class saloon with a new model.
As is typical in the industry, consumers put off buying a new 5-Series until they could have the latest edition, depressing sales in 1996 and giving a boost to results this year.
But analysts said there was no getting around the fact that BMW has assembled an attractive model mix led by the new 5-Series and the popular Z3 roadster, which is made in the U.S.
The models have helped make up for BMW's mainstay 3-Series model which has seen demand fade ahead of a new version expected to be unveiled at the Geneva car show next spring.
"BMW has always had a good strategy of staggering the introduction of new models," said Lawson at Salomon Brothers.

BMW said last week that deliveries of BMW branded cars climbed 10 percent in the first half to around 350,000 cars and that its share of the German car market climbed to 6.5 percent from 6.1 percent a year ago.
A bigger question mark for BMW is its Rover Group unit.
Rover lost 279 million marks last year, an improvement from a 335 million mark loss in 1995 and, according to Chairman Bernd Pischetsrieder, is on target to turn a profit by 2000.

But some analysts worried that the most profitable part of Rover, its Land Rover recreational vehicles, may face an uphill battle in the future with Mercedes M-Class likely to present customers a cheaper, more advanced alternative.

"Land Rover is a healthy, profitable, cash dispensing machine. Its the jewel in Rover's crown," said Peter Schmidt, analyst at Automotive Industry Data outside London. "The question is: How long can that last?"
Analysts said the first-half figures could give BMW shares a boost, but warned that as at the company's annual press conference, the firm could temper rosy figures by saying that growth will slow.
BMW shares, which stood at 1,475.00 marks on Monday afternoon, have not climbed as much this year as others in the German car industry and could be ripe to catch up, analysts said.
-- Frankfurt Newsroom, +49-69 756525
($ = 1.842 German Marks)
